summary: This proposed standard defines MIB objects for managing DS1 and E1 interfaces, the telephone-company style T1 and E1 digital links. It was replaced by RFC 2495.

eli5.summary: T1 and E1 are digital phone-line connections. This paper lists what a network manager can ask about them, such as whether they are working properly.

questions: snmp objects for t1 and e1 links
how do you monitor t1 and e1 lines
what does loss of frame mean on a t1 line
subtitle: What a network manager can observe and control on T1 and E1 telephone-company digital links.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a standard way to monitor and troubleshoot T1 and E1 telephone company digital links, and to gather performance statistics and error counts from devices that manage these links.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines SNMP management information base (MIB) objects that represent the configuration, current status, interval statistics, and total statistics for DS1 (T1) and E1 interfaces, including performance defects, error events, and failure states.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides the standardized vocabulary for tools to query and configure T1/E1 hardware. It was corrected and superseded by RFC 2495 because the original RFC 1232 had fundamental data type errors.

today: RFC 1406 was obsoleted by RFC 2495 because the original version (RFC 1232) had fundamental errors in how data types were encoded—many objects that should have been INTEGERs or Gauges were defined as Counters. RFC 2495 corrected these errors. DS1 and E1 links have faded from common use as the internet shifted to Ethernet and fiber, but the SNMP management framework and the concept of interval-based statistics collection live on in modern network equipment.

sections.title: Monitoring Telephone Company Digital Links
sections.content:
DS1 (Digital Signal level 1) is the term for T1 and E1 digital links—the 1.544 Mbps T1 lines and 2.048 Mbps E1 lines that telephone companies provide to connect offices and data centers. Before the internet became ubiquitous, these were the primary way businesses moved data across long distances.

Operating these links requires monitoring their health: knowing whether signals are strong, whether errors are occurring, and whether the link has failed entirely. This RFC defines a set of SNMP management objects that let a network manager query these devices via the standard SNMP protocol and learn exactly what is happening on each link.
sections.eli5: Your office has a phone-company digital line that brings the internet in. You need to know: is it working? How fast? Are there errors? What kind of problems is it having? This RFC lists all the questions you can ask.

sections.title: DS1 and E1 Formats and Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC covers four main DS1/E1 varieties: the AT&T D4 format, the AT&T Extended Superframe Format (ESF), and the CCITT E1 format in two versions (with and without CRC checksums). These formats differ slightly in how they handle framing, error detection, and signaling, but the MIB tries to cover all of them with a single set of objects.

The terminology is critical: the RFC defines error events (like Bipolar Violations and Line Coding Violations), performance defects (like Out of Frame and Alarm Indication Signal), and failure states (like Loss of Signal and Loss of Frame). A Line Errored Second is a one-second interval in which at least one error was detected. Severely Errored Seconds are seconds with very high error rates. Degraded Minutes are one-minute intervals where the error rate exceeds a threshold but the link is not yet unavailable.

All statistics are collected in fifteen-minute intervals, and the agent keeps up to 24 hours of history (96 intervals). There is also a rolling 24-hour total of each statistic.
sections.eli5: Different phone companies use different ways to send data on a T1 line. Some check errors one way, others another. The document lists what errors to look for on each type, and groups them into one-second and one-minute blocks to spot patterns.

sections.title: The MIB Groups and Tables
sections.content:
The MIB defines three main groups: DS1 Near End Group (mandatory), DS1 Far End Group (optional), and the Fractional Table (optional).

The Near End Group has four tables: Configuration, Current, Interval, and Total. The Configuration Table lists the type of line, the line coding algorithm, loopback configuration, transmit clock source, and other settings that identify and describe the link. The Current Table shows real-time or recently measured statistics. The Interval Table holds statistics for the last 96 fifteen-minute intervals. The Total Table holds the 24-hour rolling total.

The optional Far End Group contains statistics that come from the far end of the link—for example, if the far-end equipment sends error reports back to the near end via a facilities data link. This requires special support on both ends and is not always available.

Each table row is indexed by dsx1LineIndex, which uniquely identifies a DS1 interface on a device.
sections.eli5: The data is organized into tables. One table says what kind of line it is. One table shows what is happening right now. One keeps a day's worth of history in 15-minute snapshots. One adds it all up.

sections.title: Error Types and Failure States
sections.content:
The RFC defines several categories of error conditions. Line Coding Violations are violations of the signal encoding rules—for example, a pulse that should not be there (Bipolar Violation) or too many consecutive zero bits without a pulse (Excessive Zeroes). Path Coding Violations are frame synchronization errors in D4 and E1-noCRC formats, or CRC errors in ESF and E1-CRC formats.

A Performance Defect is a larger problem than a single error. An Out of Frame defect means the receiver has lost synchronization with the frame boundaries. An Alarm Indication Signal defect occurs when the receiver detects an unframed "all ones" pattern. A Controlled Slip is when the receiver must skip or repeat payload bits to stay synchronized if there is a timing difference between the transmitter and receiver.

A Failure State is a serious condition that makes the link unavailable for service. Loss of Frame is declared when the Out of Frame defect has persisted for several seconds. Loss of Signal is declared when the receiver detects many consecutive bit positions with no pulses. Far End Alarm is when the far end equipment sends a signal saying it has detected a failure (the T1 world calls this "Yellow Alarm"; the E1 world calls it "Distant Alarm"). A Loopback Pseudo-Failure is declared when the near end has put the line into a loopback test mode—this is not a real failure, but the link is out of service.
sections.eli5: Small hiccups are errors: a bit got corrupted, a timing pulse arrived wrong. Big problems are failures: the whole signal went away, or the frame got scrambled. The MIB counts both and reports them.

sections.title: Interface Indexing and Configuration
sections.content:
A device may have DS1 interfaces connected to the outside network, and possibly also internal interfaces that connect the SNMP agent to the DS1 card itself (if the agent is on a host separate from the DS1 device). The RFC introduces two index values: dsx1IfIndex (the interface index in the standard MIB-II Interfaces table) and dsx1LineIndex (a unique identifier for each physical DS1 line on the device).

In the simple case, a device's DS1 interfaces map one-to-one with its external interfaces, and dsx1IfIndex equals dsx1LineIndex equals ifIndex. When an SNMP agent on a router proxies for a shelf of separate DS1 devices, the agent assigns unique dsx1LineIndex values to all DS1 lines (both router-side and network-side of each circuit), while dsx1IfIndex reflects only the router's own interfaces.

The Configuration Table also lists the line type (D4, ESF, E1-CRC, etc.), the line coding (AMI, B8ZS, HDB3, etc.), loopback configuration, and a circuit identifier string that the vendor may populate with useful information for troubleshooting.
sections.eli5: When a device has multiple T1 lines, you need a way to tell them apart. One naming scheme works for simple boxes; a different scheme works when you are managing a big shelf of them from a separate computer.

viz.caption: Categories of DS1/E1 problems and what they mean

items.title: Line Coding Violation
items.text: A single bit violated the encoding rules (Bipolar Violation or Excessive Zeroes).

items.title: Out of Frame
items.text: Frame alignment was lost; the receiver cannot find the start of frames.

items.title: Loss of Signal
items.text: No pulses detected for many bit positions; the physical signal may be dead.

items.title: Loopback
items.text: The equipment is in test mode, sending traffic back to itself instead of across the link.

items.title: Far End Alarm
items.text: The remote end detected a failure and sent back an alarm signal (Yellow or Distant Alarm).

items.title: Controlled Slip
items.text: Timing was out of sync, so the receiver skipped or repeated payload bits.
